column3: Demand is 99 Mt and supply is 96 Mt. What is the market balance (supply − demand)?
column4: WHY: 96 − 99 = -3 Mt. Positive is surplus; negative is deficit.

column3: All else equal, a persistent supply deficit tends to…
column4: WHY: A deficit must be met from inventories or demand destruction, which usually tightens the market.

column3: Stocks are 32 Mt and annual demand is 260 Mt. Approximate days of cover?
column4: WHY: 32 ÷ (260 ÷ 365) = 44.9 days of cover.

column3: Nearby futures above deferred futures is called…
column4: WHY: Backwardation is an inverted curve: nearby value exceeds deferred value.

column3: A steep contango can economically reward…
column4: WHY: If the deferred premium exceeds storage, finance and losses, storing and carrying inventory can be attractive.

column3: Destination value is $720/t. Freight $35/t and handling $12/t. What is the implied origin netback?
Two markets show the same benchmark price, but one has much higher freight to reach your buyer. Which matters for the physical decision?
column4: WHY: Physical arbitrage is decided by all-in delivered economics, not the headline benchmark alone.

column3: Product value $740/t, feedstock $650/t, processing cost $55/t. Simple processing margin?
A bullish market view and a long physical exposure are…
column4: WHY: A view is a belief. Exposure is what your P&L actually does when the market moves.

column3: A strong analysis note should separate facts, assumptions and conclusions because…
column4: WHY: Separating evidence from assumptions makes a market view testable instead of narrative-only.

column3: Days of cover fall from 45 to 22 while the balance stays in deficit. What does that tell you?
column4: WHY: Cover measures how long the market can absorb a shock. Low cover plus a deficit is the setup for a violent move on small news.

column3: A balance shows a surplus but prices keep rising. What is the most likely explanation?
column4: WHY: A global balance hides location and quality. Material stranded behind a bottleneck does not relieve a tight consuming region.

column3: Why is a netback more useful than a headline benchmark when choosing where to sell?
column4: WHY: Two destinations can show the same benchmark and pay you very differently once the route is paid for.

column3: Processing margins collapse to near zero across an industry. What usually follows?
column4: WHY: Negative margins are self-correcting: plants cut runs, and the feedstock and product balances both shift.

column3: You have a strong bearish view but the curve is in steep backwardation. What does the curve tell you?
column4: WHY: Backwardation is the market paying for immediacy. It can coexist with a weak forward view, and it makes being short the front expensive.

column3: Which evidence would most change a supply–demand view?
column4: WHY: Views should move on quantities, not on price action that may simply be positioning.

column3: Why do desks track floating storage separately from onshore stocks?
column4: WHY: Where inventory sits changes when and where it can be delivered, which is what the physical market prices.

column3: A producing region loses export capacity for two months. What is the first-order effect?
column4: WHY: Supply that cannot move is not supply. Logistics failures show up as spreads before they show up in the balance.

column3: What is the honest limit of a supply–demand balance?
column4: WHY: Balances are directional tools. Treating them as precise is how people become confidently wrong.

column3: Capacity is 93 Mt a year and utilisation is 78%. Approximate output?
column4: WHY: 93 × 78% = 72.5 Mt. Utilisation is where a supply forecast usually goes wrong.

column3: Demand is 73 Mt and grows 3% next year. Demand next year?
column4: WHY: 73 × (1 + 3%) = 75.2 Mt. A few points of demand growth on a large base can absorb an entire new plant.

column3: Stocks fall from 40 Mt to 32 Mt over 30 days. Average inventory draw per day?
column4: WHY: 8 ÷ 30 = 0.27 Mt/day.

column3: Nearby futures are $710/t and deferred futures are $720/t. What is nearby minus deferred? Use a negative number for contango.
Destination A pays $740/t with $30/t freight. Destination B pays $780/t with $45/t freight. By how much does A's netback exceed B's?

Initial demand is 99 Mt and supply 97 Mt. A 6 Mt supply outage occurs and demand is revised by +1 Mt. New balance (supply − demand)?
Why compare inventories with their normal seasonal range rather than only with last month?
column4: WHY: A normal seasonal draw can look bullish in isolation. Context tells you whether inventory behaviour is actually unusual.

column3: Deferred value is $16/t above prompt. Storage costs $5/t and finance $8/t. Net carry before losses?
When does a regional arbitrage normally close?
column4: WHY: Arbitrage is an all-in delivered comparison. Once the netback advantage disappears, the trade stops paying.

column3: Why can a small change in processing yield matter more than a small move in the headline benchmark?
column4: WHY: A few yield points applied to large throughput can move the processing margin materially.

column3: A market view should include an invalidation condition because…
column4: WHY: A thesis without a falsifiable trigger becomes a story that can survive any evidence.

column3: Sell $780/t, buy $720/t, freight $35/t, finance $11/t. Net trading margin?
A buyer may choose the pricing month after shipment, while your purchase month is fixed. That clause gives the buyer…
column4: WHY: The buyer controls timing of price fixation while you carry the mismatch; that option has economic value.

column3: Which trade is usually better, all else equal?
column4: WHY: Return on capital and time matter. A slightly smaller margin can be far better if capital turns much faster.

column3: Margin is $15/t on 40,000 t. Gross contribution?
You can buy FOB A or FOB B. What should decide the origin choice for a fixed CIF sale?
column4: WHY: A lower FOB price can be worse if freight, quality or execution costs more than offset it.

column3: Why can “more volume” reduce desk quality?
column4: WHY: Scarce capital, limits and operational capacity should be allocated to the best risk-adjusted opportunities.

column3: Gross margin $35/t, quality claim $8/t, demurrage $10/t, FX impact +$2/t. Final margin?
A good trader should treat an unpriced operational risk as…
column4: WHY: Commercial pricing should reflect risks you actually retain, even if the final amount is uncertain.

column3: If two deals have equal expected profit, prefer the one with…
column4: WHY: Expected profit alone is incomplete; downside, liquidity and capital efficiency matter.

column3: The core question before accepting a physical trade is…
column4: WHY: The merchant margin only survives if the residual risks are identified and priced.

column3: A buyer asks for a ±10% quantity option at their choice. What have you given away?
column4: WHY: Operational tolerances are options. If you do not price them, the counterparty exercises them against you.

column3: Your purchase prices on the month of loading and your sale on the month of discharge. What have you created?
column4: WHY: Matching volumes is not matching risk. Different pricing windows leave you long or short the spread between them.

column3: Which deal would a disciplined desk prefer?
column4: WHY: Margin that cannot be collected or executed is not margin. Volume is a vanity metric on a physical desk.

column3: You can nominate one of three discharge ports. What is that worth?
column4: WHY: Destination flexibility is one of the most valuable and most under-priced features in a physical contract.

column3: Why do desks look at the book rather than each trade alone?
column4: WHY: Two trades that look risky alone can be flat together, and two that look safe can compound.

column3: A counterparty offers a price well above the market for prompt delivery. What should you check first?
column4: WHY: An unusually good price usually carries an unusually good reason. Often it is distress, and distress carries credit risk.

column3: What does "washout" mean in a physical contract?
column4: WHY: A washout closes a contract financially when delivery no longer makes sense for either side.

column3: Your margin depends on a quality premium the buyer disputes on arrival. What was the mistake?
column4: WHY: Quality disputes are decided by the words agreed beforehand, not by who is more certain afterwards.

column3: Why is a signed recap not the same as a concluded contract?
column4: WHY: Most commercial arguments live in the gap between the recap and the full contract.

column3: You improve the netback by $16/t on 30,000 t. Total contribution?
column4: WHY: 30,000 × 16 = $480,000. Small per-tonne gains matter because tonnage is large.

column3: A contract lets the buyer choose the loading window inside a two-month range. Who benefits?
column4: WHY: Every flexibility belongs to someone. If the contract does not say it is yours, assume it is being used against you.

column3: Buy $660/t, sell $710/t, all-in costs $29/t, on 45,000 t. Total net contribution?
column4: WHY: (710 − 660 − 29) × 45,000 = $945,000. The costs line is where headline spreads go to die.

column3: A buyer has a +10% quantity option on 30,000 t at a fixed sale price. If replacement supply is $10/t more expensive when they exercise the extra volume, downside on the optional tonnes?
Purchase prices in Month 1 and sale prices in Month 2 on 30,000 t. The Month-2 minus Month-1 spread moves $8/t against you. Approximate timing P&L?
Origin A gives a delivered margin of $22/t and Origin B $20/t on 60,000 t. Contribution advantage of A over B?
A deal earns $14/t on 30,000 t, ties up $24,000,000 for 90 days. Approximate annualised return on capital?
Gross expected margin is $24/t. A 10% chance of an execution problem would cost $60/t. Simple expected margin after that risk?
Why should a trader price a quantity tolerance explicitly?
column4: WHY: A tolerance changes how much you may have to source or place at future market conditions.

column3: You are economically long the Month-2 versus Month-1 spread on 60,000 t. Month 1 settles $740/t and Month 2 $730/t. Spread P&L?
A location arbitrage is real only when…
column4: WHY: Physical arbitrage is a chain of executable costs and rights, not a screen-price comparison.

column3: Headline margin $30/t, finance $5/t, expected credit cost $8/t and execution reserve $7/t. Risk-adjusted margin?
Voyage freight is $600,000 for 35,000 t. Freight per tonne?
Laycan is…
column4: WHY: Laycan defines when the vessel must be ready to load under the charter.

column3: 2 days exceed allowed laytime. Demurrage is $18,000/day. Cost?
A vessel arrives before laycan. Must the charterer automatically start laytime?
column4: WHY: Arrival alone is not enough; laytime depends on the charter wording and valid notice/readiness conditions.

column3: Time-charter hire $16,000/day for 30 days plus bunkers $650,000. Approximate voyage vessel cost?
For a fixed CIF sale, an unfixed freight rate is economically…
column4: WHY: You fixed the delivered sale price but not the transport cost, so rising freight erodes your margin.

column3: Why might a larger vessel be worse despite a lower $/t headline rate?
column4: WHY: The vessel must fit the parcel, ports, draft and timing; headline freight is not the only constraint.

column3: You sold CIF on 30,000 t with freight budget $32/t. Market freight rises by $12/t before fixing. P&L impact?
column4: WHY: The extra freight cost is 30,000 × $12 = $360,000 loss.

column3: Deadfreight is typically associated with…
column4: WHY: If the charterer supplies less cargo than contracted, the owner may claim freight on the unused capacity.

column3: The freight decision belongs at quotation time because…
column4: WHY: Delivered commodity economics and shipping economics are inseparable on a physical trade.

column3: An owner refuses your cargo despite a freight rate above the last done. Why might that be rational?
column4: WHY: Owners compare in dollars per day. A high rate on a slow, badly positioned voyage can still lose to a lower rate on a fast one.

column3: Why does a laycan that is too narrow cost you money even if the ship arrives?
column4: WHY: Flexibility is worth money to the person who has it. Giving it up is a real cost even when nothing goes wrong.

column3: You are quoted the same rate for two routes of equal distance. What still differs?
column4: WHY: Distance is one input. Days are the currency, and port and canal time consume days without earning them.

column3: Why is demurrage often a negotiation rather than an arithmetic result?
column4: WHY: The daily rate is agreed; what is contested is how many hours qualify.

column3: Valid NOR has been tendered, laytime has started, the allowed laytime is exhausted and no charterparty exception applies. Port congestion continues. What normally follows?
column4: WHY: Once valid laytime is exhausted, qualifying time normally runs on demurrage unless the charterparty provides an applicable exception.

column3: Bunker prices rise sharply between your indication and the fixture. What happens?
column4: WHY: A freight indication assumes a fuel price. Once fuel moves, a stale indication is not a price.

column3: Why do desks watch the ballast position of the fleet, not just the freight index?
column4: WHY: Freight is priced by the marginal available ship, and availability is local.

column3: What does a sub-let of a time-chartered vessel expose you to?
column4: WHY: Chartering in and out builds a chain, and you sit in the middle of it holding both obligations.

column3: Freight is $28/t on 35,000 t. Total freight?
column4: WHY: 35,000 × 28 = $980,000. On a cargo worth tens of millions this is often several percent of the value.

column3: Hire is $22,000/day for 23 days, plus $209,000 of port costs. Total cost before bunkers?
column4: WHY: 23 × $22,000 + $209,000 = $715,000. Bunkers come on top, and they are usually the largest and most volatile piece.

column3: Gross freight revenue $800,000, bunkers $300,000, port/other voyage costs $240,000, total voyage 45 days. Approximate TCE?
A time-chartered vessel waits 2 days before the agreed loading window. Hire is $22,000/day. Direct waiting-hire cost?
A laycan window spans 6 days. Your vessel ETA uncertainty is ±2 days. Ignoring other delays, how many days of nominal window remain beyond the two-sided ETA uncertainty?
column4: WHY: 6 − 2 × 2 = 4 days.

column3: What must be checked before treating a Notice of Readiness as valid?
column4: WHY: Laytime consequences depend on a valid NOR under the actual charterparty wording.

column3: Statement of Facts shows 84 elapsed hours. 12 hours are excluded and allowed laytime is 96 hours. Demurrage is $26,000/day. Demurrage amount?
Under a typical time charter, which cost is normally for the charterer rather than the owner?
column4: WHY: Time charterers normally control commercial employment and pay voyage-related bunkers, while owners retain technical operation and crew.

column3: A vessel ballasts 6 days, consuming 30 t/day of fuel at $750/t. Ballast bunker cost?
Route requires 16 laden days, 6 ballast days and 8 port days. Total voyage duration?
A charterer exposed to rising freight may use an FFA primarily to…
column4: WHY: Freight derivatives target market-rate exposure; they do not remove operational or basis risk between the actual voyage and the index.

column3: In tanker freight, Worldscale 100 means…
column4: WHY: Worldscale points are percentage points of the route-specific published flat rate.

column3: Worldscale flat rate is $18/t and the fixture is WS100 on 120,000 t. Approximate freight?
You fund $4,000,000 of cargo for 60 days at 8% a year, on a 360-day basis. What is the interest cost?
A documentary letter of credit primarily helps the seller by…
column4: WHY: A compliant LC can materially improve payment security, but only if documents meet its conditions.

column3: Counterparty limit $8,000,000, current exposure $2,000,000. Remaining headroom?
column4: WHY: $8,000,000 − $2,000,000 = $6,000,000. Headroom is what you can still trade with them before the limit stops you.

column3: Selling 60 days open account instead of cash against documents should normally…
column4: WHY: Longer unsecured terms use capital and increase default exposure.

column3: Eligible inventory is $6,000,000 and borrowing-base advance rate is 75%. Maximum borrowing against it?
A credit limit is best thought of as…
column4: WHY: Limits cap acceptable exposure. Using them consumes scarce capacity that should earn enough return.

column3: A sale earns $25/t but adds 90 days of financing on $760/t at 7% p.a. Incremental finance cost per tonne?
Which event can create a margin call even when your physical trade is economically hedged?
column4: WHY: Hedges can create liquidity needs before offsetting physical cash arrives. Economic hedge does not mean zero funding risk.

column3: Documents under an LC are discrepant. The key risk is…
column4: WHY: Documentary compliance is central to LC payment.

column3: Best credit-adjusted trade is usually…
column4: WHY: Commercial return must be assessed after credit and capital costs, not before them.

column3: A bank lends against your inventory at an 80% advance rate. What happens if the price falls 30%?
column4: WHY: Asset-based lending is procyclical: the collateral and the credit available fall together, which is why a price crash becomes a funding crisis.

column3: Why does a seller ask for a letter of credit to be confirmed?
column4: WHY: An LC is only as good as the bank behind it. Confirmation moves that risk to a bank the seller is willing to face.

column3: What is the practical difference between a documentary LC and a standby LC?
column4: WHY: One is how you expect to be paid; the other is what you fall back on when you are not.

column3: Your documents are refused for a discrepancy. What are your realistic options?
column4: WHY: Banks are entitled to refuse on strict compliance. Most discrepancies are resolved commercially, which hands leverage to the buyer.

column3: Why does a desk measure days sales outstanding?
column4: WHY: Every extra day of receivable is financed. On thin margins, collection speed can matter as much as price.

column3: A supplier offers you a discount if you prepay before delivery. What have you become economically?
column4: WHY: Prepayment moves cash before performance. Until cargo is delivered or collateral is realised, you carry supplier credit/performance exposure.

column3: What does assignment of receivables give a lender?
column4: WHY: Structured trade finance works by attaching the lender to specific cash flows rather than to your balance sheet alone.

column3: Credit insurance covers your buyer. Why is it not the same as being paid?
column4: WHY: Insurance changes who you are exposed to and when you get paid, not whether the exposure exists.

column3: Why do desks net exposures with a counterparty across contracts?
column4: WHY: Without enforceable netting, you are exposed gross even when the economics offset.

column3: Financing $670/t of cargo for 45 days at 8% a year on a 360-day basis. Finance cost per tonne?
column4: WHY: 670 × 8% × 45/360 = $6.7/t. Compare this with the margin before agreeing longer payment terms.

column3: Confirmed LC amount $8,000,000, confirmation fee 80 bps p.a. for 120 days on a 360-day basis. Approximate fee?
A bank discounts a $5,000,000 deferred-payment LC at 5% p.a. for 120 days on a 360-day basis. Approximate discount cost?
You sold 15,000 t open account. The mark-to-market moves $20/t in your favour before payment, increasing replacement exposure to the buyer. Additional exposure?
Why are payment terms part of the commodity price?
column4: WHY: A $/t margin is not comparable until you account for how long cash and credit are tied up.

column3: Inventory days 30, receivable days 40, supplier payable days 50. Approximate cash conversion cycle?
Why does a borrowing base apply advance rates or haircuts to collateral?
column4: WHY: The lender advances less than face value because collateral can fall in value or cost money to realise.

column3: Eligible collateral $12,000,000, advance rate 75%, existing borrowing $10,000,000. Additional borrowing availability?
Expected credit loss is useful commercially because…
column4: WHY: A simplified expected-loss charge helps compare two trades with different counterparty quality.

column3: A high-margin deal that consumes nearly all remaining counterparty limit should be judged on…
column4: WHY: Credit limit is scarce balance-sheet capacity and should earn an adequate return.

column3: Exposure $4,000,000, one-year default probability 2%, loss-given-default 60%. Simplified expected loss?
Gross margin $30/t, finance $6/t, expected credit cost $8/t and capital charge $4/t. Credit-adjusted margin?
Long physical 80,000 t and short futures 50,000 t. Net flat-price exposure?
A one-day 99% VaR of $3m means…
column4: WHY: VaR is a percentile threshold under modelling assumptions, not a maximum-loss bound.

column3: Why run stress tests if you already have VaR?
column4: WHY: Stress tests explore tail moves, broken correlations and specific operational/market shocks.

column3: You hedge a physical grade with a related but different futures contract. The residual is mainly…
column4: WHY: An imperfect proxy hedge leaves risk that physical and futures values diverge.

column3: Available liquidity $14,000,000. Margin call $7,000,000 and other near-term cash needs $10,000,000. Liquidity headroom?
A profitable book can still fail because of…
column4: WHY: Timing matters. Margin calls and supplier payments can arrive before customer receipts.

column3: Ten exposures with different customer names but the same terminal create…
column4: WHY: Shared chokepoints create correlated losses despite different legal counterparties.

column3: Desk net-long limit 60,000 t; current net-long 80,000 t. Minimum reduction needed?
When a hard risk limit is breached, the correct first principle is…
column4: WHY: Limits only work when breaches trigger transparent governance and action.

column3: A good hedge should be assessed on…
column4: WHY: Hedge P&L in isolation is misleading; the combined physical-plus-hedge position is what matters.

column3: Your VaR is comfortably inside the limit and the desk still loses more than VaR in a day. What went wrong?
column4: WHY: A 95% VaR is expected to be exceeded about one day in twenty. Being surprised by that means it was being read as a ceiling.

column3: Why can a desk be within every price limit and still fail?
column4: WHY: The risks that end desks are usually cash and counterparties, and neither appears in a price limit.

column3: What is the purpose of an independent risk function?
column4: WHY: The control only works because the person applying it does not benefit from the position.

column3: A correlation that has held for five years breaks in a week. Why is that predictable?
column4: WHY: Statistical relationships are calm-market artefacts. Stress tests exist because of this.

column3: What does a stop-loss discipline actually protect against?
column4: WHY: It is a control on behaviour more than on the market. Its value is that it is decided before the loss.

column3: Why report position and exposure separately?
column4: WHY: A large position can carry small exposure if it is hedged, and a small one can carry large exposure if it is not.

column3: A single grade, single port, single buyer trade is 40% of the book. Which limit catches this?
column4: WHY: Concentration hides inside an acceptable total. It needs its own constraint.

column3: What is model risk on a commodity desk?
column4: WHY: A model is a set of assumptions with numbers attached. When the assumptions fail, the numbers stay confident.

column3: Why does an operational error belong in the risk report?
column4: WHY: On physical desks, execution failures are a routine and material source of loss.

column3: You are long 30,000 t at $7750/t. Estimated one-day price volatility is 2%. Using a 95% factor of 1.645, what is the one-day parametric VaR?
column4: WHY: 30,000 × $7750 × 2% × 1.645 ≈ $7,649,250. VaR is a model estimate, not a maximum-loss bound.

column3: Why should a risk report show the worst historical drawdown alongside VaR?
column4: WHY: History is a poor forecast but an honest reminder. It anchors the conversation in events rather than in parameters.

column3: Your net long limit is 60,000 t. You are long 90,000 t physical and short 90,000 t futures. By how many tonnes are you over the limit? Use a negative number if you are inside it.
column4: WHY: Net is 90,000 − 90,000 = 0 t, against a 60,000 t limit: -60,000 t. Limits are checked on the net, not the gross.

column3: Why can gross position and net flat-price exposure tell different stories?
column4: WHY: A desk can be flat to price and still have large settlement, basis, financing and execution obligations.

column3: Long physical 60,000 t. Short proxy hedge 50,000 t with hedge delta 1. Approximate residual equivalent exposure?
Stress scenario: a 30,000 t net-long position faces a $60/t price fall. Flat-price stress loss?
Stress losses: price $3,000,000, freight $2,000,000, counterparty $6,000,000. Combined scenario loss?

Physical leg gains $6,000,000 while hedge loses $6,000,000. Combined hedge result?
Why can margin calls create a crisis on a profitable hedged trade?
column4: WHY: Liquidity timing, not only final economics, determines whether a desk survives the path to settlement.

column3: Available cash $15,000,000; margin calls $8,000,000, supplier payments $10,000,000, customer delay reserve $4,000,000. Liquidity headroom?
Long physical inventory exposed to a price fall is commonly hedged by…
column4: WHY: Short futures offset the downside of long physical flat-price exposure.

column3: You are short futures on 20,000 t and futures rise $10/t. Futures P&L?
column4: WHY: A short loses when price rises: 20,000 × $10 = $200,000 loss.

column3: After a good futures hedge, which risk may remain?
column4: WHY: Futures hedge the benchmark exposure they match; physical differential and timing can still move.

column3: A fixed-price purchase plus a floating-price sale leaves you primarily…
column4: WHY: You have locked the cost but not the revenue benchmark, so falling prices can hurt.

column3: Buying a put option gives you…
column4: WHY: A put creates a floor-like payoff but the option premium is the cost of that asymmetry.

column3: Put premium is $6/t on 15,000 t. Upfront option premium cost?
An option delta of +0.40 means, approximately…
column4: WHY: Delta is a local price sensitivity, not an exact probability or time measure.

column3: Why can hedge ratios be less than 100%?
column4: WHY: The economically appropriate hedge depends on the exposure actually being offset.

column3: A swap is useful when you want to…
column4: WHY: Commodity swaps commonly transform price index exposure without moving physical goods.

column3: Best hedge design starts from…
column4: WHY: You hedge the risk created by the physical contract—not an abstract market view.

column3: Why do commodity desks often use Asian (average price) options rather than plain vanilla?
column4: WHY: A hedge should match how the cargo is priced. Hedging an averaged exposure with a single-date option leaves a timing mismatch.

column3: You buy a put to protect a long inventory. What is the worst case?
column4: WHY: A bought option has known, limited cost. That is what you pay for compared with a futures hedge.

column3: What is a zero-cost collar?
column4: WHY: It is not free: you paid with the upside you gave away, which is a real cost if the market rallies.

column3: Why does a swap suit a refiner with steady monthly volumes?
column4: WHY: Swaps settle against an average and are usually bilateral, which fits a regular physical programme.

column3: Implied volatility rises sharply while the price is unchanged. What has happened?
column4: WHY: Volatility is a traded quantity of its own. Hedging costs can rise without the underlying moving at all.

column3: What does delta tell a hedger?
column4: WHY: Delta is how much of a futures position the option is equivalent to right now, and it changes as the market moves.

column3: Why is selling options to earn premium dangerous for a physical desk?
column4: WHY: Writing options converts a trading business into an insurance business, usually without the capital to match.

column3: What is a basis swap used for?
column4: WHY: It targets exactly the risk a plain futures hedge leaves behind.

column3: A spread option pays on the difference between two prices. Where does that fit?
column4: WHY: Refining and arbitrage margins are spreads, so the natural hedge is an instrument on the spread.

column3: You hold options on 15,000 t with a delta of 0.45. How many tonnes of futures do they currently behave like?
column4: WHY: 15,000 × 0.45 = 6,750 t. Delta changes as the market moves, so the hedge has to be revisited.

column3: You buy a put at $6/t and sell a call at $6/t on 40,000 t. Net premium paid? Use a negative number if you receive it.
column4: WHY: (6 − 6) × 40,000 = $0. A collar is only "zero cost" when the two premiums happen to match.

column3: You are short 40 lots of 50 t and the futures price rises $38/t. Variation margin due?
column4: WHY: 40 × 50 × 38 = $76,000, payable in cash now while the physical gain is still unrealised.

column3: Why must hedge sizing start from contract units and lot sizes?
column4: WHY: Execution requires translating physical exposure into actual exchange lots and accepting any rounding residual.

column3: Variation margin belongs in hedge design because…
column4: WHY: Derivative settlement timing can be as important as terminal P&L for a physical merchant.

column3: Exposure is 25,000 t and the hedge contract is 50 t per lot. Approximate whole lots required?
A cross-hedge should be monitored for…
column4: WHY: A proxy can behave well in normal markets and diverge when the underlying physical market is stressed.
